A Vietnamese noodle soup of clear broth, flat rice noodles, herbs and meat, usually beef. It took shape in the north of Vietnam, around Nam Định and Hanoi, in the early 1900s.

Its exact origins are argued over. Two influences are clear. Under French rule, cattle were slaughtered for beef more often, leaving bones for broth; some link the name to the French pot-au-feu. Chinese cooks and traders brought rice noodles and spices. The broth is simmered for hours with charred onion and ginger, star anise and cinnamon.

When Vietnam was split at the Geneva Conference of 1954, many northerners moved south and took phở with them. In Saigon it gained bean sprouts, basil, lime and sauces on the side, while Hanoi kept a plainer bowl.

After the fall of Saigon in 1975, refugees opened phở shops in the United States, Australia, France and Canada. It became one of the best known foods of Asia and a symbol of Vietnam abroad.
sum: A Vietnamese noodle soup of clear broth, flat rice noodles, herbs and meat, usually beef. It took shape in the north of Vietnam, around Nam Định and Hanoi, in the early 1900s.
